cover.headline: India's value-shopping leader, priced ahead of its margins
cover.lead: Meesho is India's largest e-commerce platform by buyers and orders: 274 million people bought on it in the year to Jun-2026, mostly outside the big cities, from ~1 million small sellers who pay no commission. Order value delivered (NMV) grew 34% in Q1FY27 to ₹11,614 cr and the marketplace loss narrowed to 1.2% of NMV. The stock has doubled from ₹111 at the Dec-2025 IPO to ₹{{P.last|num}} and trades at ~1.49x next year's NMV, against a median of 1.23x since January. Our sum of the parts gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with SELL.** Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}} ({{scen.bear.upside|chg}}). The street's median target is ₹212.5.

arguments.h: The biggest buyer base in Indian e-commerce, still growing fast
arguments.p: 274 million annual buyers (+29%) and 1.04 million sellers (+81%); NMV +34% in Q1FY27. Zero commission and Valmo logistics make it the cheapest place to sell. Management guides to ~25% NMV growth a year for five years; we use 26% to FY29E.

arguments.h: Profit is a FY28-29 story, and slow by design
arguments.p: Contribution margin recovered to 4.6% of NMV, but fixed costs take 5.8%, so the marketplace still lost 1.2% of NMV. Meesho passes logistics savings on to buyers; margins depend on ads. We forecast break-even in FY28E and 1.3% of NMV in FY29E, below the street.

arguments.h: Cash-rich, but the register is in flux
arguments.p: ₹6,521 cr of cash and negative working capital mean no new money is needed. But venture investors (~40%) have been selling since the Jun-2026 lock-in expiry, and ₹2,072 cr of contested tax demands plus a GST question over Valmo hang over the cash.

arguments.h: Valuation: the stock already pays above its own history
arguments.p: At ₹228 the market pays 1.49x next year's NMV, against a median of 1.23x since January. At our derived 1.2x Sep-28E NMV the sum of the parts gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): SELL. The street's median target is ₹212.5; its bulls (Jefferies 1.6x NMV) need margins we do not yet see.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): NMV growth will look soft because the big sale moved into Q3, and growth spending rises; the test is Q2 and Q3 together.
Contribution margin: can it keep rising from 4.6% of NMV as ads grow, while logistics savings are passed on to buyers?
Supply: venture investors still hold ~40% after the Jun-2026 lock-in expiry; block sales have continued every month.
GST on Valmo's freight (InGovern letter to SEBI, Jul-2026) and ₹2,072 cr of contested income-tax demands.

sections.title: A zero-commission marketplace for Bharat, paid for by delivery fees and ads

blocks.p: Meesho runs an online marketplace where small sellers (mostly unbranded apparel, home, kitchen and beauty products) sell to price-conscious buyers, most of them outside India's big cities. Sellers pay **no commission**. Meesho earns instead from (1) **fulfilment fees**: sellers pay for delivery, which Meesho arranges through **Valmo**, its own logistics platform that pools thousands of small truckers, sorting centres and couriers, or through third-party couriers; (2) **advertising**: sellers pay to rank higher in search and feeds (about two-thirds of sellers by GMV advertise); and (3) platform and other fees. Its headline measure is **NMV**, the value of orders actually delivered and kept, after discounts.

blocks.callout: **Two numbers matter most.** Contribution margin (what is left from revenue after delivery, payments and order-handling costs) shows whether each order makes money: 4.6% of NMV in Q1FY27. Below it sit costs that do not scale with orders (marketing 2.1% of NMV, servers 1.9%, staff and other 1.7%). The business breaks even when contribution margin exceeds those costs; in Q1FY27 the gap was 1.2% of NMV.

sections.title: From reseller app to India's biggest marketplace by buyers, with an expensive move home

blocks.p: Meesho started in 2015 as an app for "resellers" who shared products on WhatsApp. It became a direct marketplace, cut seller commissions to zero (FY23) and built its own logistics platform, Valmo. Three corporate events shape today's numbers: the 2024-25 move of the parent company from the US to India (expensive: ~₹3,800 cr of one-off costs and tax); the Dec-2025 IPO; and the Jun-2026 end of the pre-IPO lock-in, which turned venture investors into steady sellers.

blocks.callout: **What this means:** the venture-funded years are over: since FY24 Meesho has grown on its own cash, and the IPO money largely replaced the ₹3,344 cr spent on moving home. The four largest venture investors alone held 42% of the shares at Mar-2026, and pre-IPO holders have been selling since the lock-in ended; that supply, not dilution, is the near-term cost to shareholders.

sections.title: A huge, under-served market, contested by the deepest pockets in Indian retail

blocks.p: India's e-commerce market is about ₹6 lakh crore (US$70 bn) of GMV, only ~7% of retail against 34% in China (Redseer, cited in the FY26 annual report). Unbranded and regional products are more than 70% of retail spending, sold by 55-60 million small sellers who are mostly offline. Penetration in Tier 2+ towns was ~4% in FY25 against ~14% in the top eight and Tier 1 cities; electronics is ~37% penetrated, everyday categories (apparel, home, beauty) far less. Internet users (818-853 million in FY25) are projected to approach 1 billion by FY30, and online shoppers to roughly double (Redseer).

Meesho competes for the value shopper with Flipkart (and its value app Shopsy), Amazon (Amazon Bazaar, its low-price storefront) and Reliance (Ajio, JioMart), and, for everyday essentials, with quick-commerce apps. None of the rivals is listed in India, so their economics cannot be read from filings. Meesho's edge is cost: zero commission for sellers, the cheapest delivery through Valmo, and a buyer base that is ~85% outside the top eight cities (Ambit, Sep-2026). Nomura (Sep-2026) flags rising competition from the horizontals and quick commerce as the main risk to margins.

sections.title: Each order makes money; the fixed costs still eat it (gap: 1.2% of NMV)

blocks.p: The marketplace is 99.9% of revenue. Its economics are simple. **Contribution margin** is what is left from Meesho's revenue after the costs of each order (delivery, payment gateway, customer support): 4.6% of NMV in Q1FY27, ₹531 cr. From that Meesho pays costs that do not rise with each order: growth spending (marketing and user acquisition, 2.1% of NMV), servers and software (1.9%) and staff and other costs (1.7%), together 5.8% (flat on the quarter, down 0.37pp in a year). The difference is the marketplace adjusted EBITDA: -1.2% of NMV.

blocks.p: **How the gap closes.** Management names two levers: (1) ads, which cost almost nothing to serve, so every rupee of ad revenue lifts contribution margin; and (2) restoring the logistics margin that fell in FY26 (Meesho charges sellers more for delivery than it pays partners), after which logistics savings are passed on as lower prices. On the cost side, AI tools have "more than doubled" engineering productivity (Q1FY27 letter) and fixed costs fell 0.4pp of NMV in a year. We assume break-even in FY28E and 1.3% of NMV in FY29E; Citi has 2.1% in FY29E, Jefferies and Axis Capital ~3% only by FY30E, MOFSL 3.75% by FY31E.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the unit economics work (FY24 showed a 5.6% contribution margin and positive free cash flow at a smaller scale), but Meesho chooses to reinvest efficiency gains in lower prices and user acquisition. That is a sound strategy for a market leader in a land grab, but it means margins will rise slowly. The bull case needs ads to scale toward the 3-4% of NMV that global marketplaces earn; J.P. Morgan puts Meesho's ad take rate at ~1.8%.

sections.title: Valmo makes Meesho the cheapest place to sell; ads must make it profitable

blocks.p: **Valmo** is Meesho's logistics platform. It does not own trucks or warehouses: it pools thousands of small first-mile, sorting, line-haul and last-mile operators and assigns each order to the cheapest reliable route. Sellers pay a delivery fee, which is most of Meesho's revenue. In Q2-Q3FY26, when India's third-party courier market consolidated, Meesho moved volume onto Valmo very quickly; the new partners and sort nodes ran inefficiently, and contribution margin fell from 4.4% to 2.3% of NMV without fees being raised. By Q4FY26 it was back to 4.0%, and to 4.6% in Q1FY27. Cost per delivered order fell another ~₹1 in Q1FY27 even after fuel and minimum-wage increases, which were passed through.

**Tax structure under scrutiny.** Much of Valmo now runs through Valmo Transportation Pvt Ltd, registered as a Goods Transport Agency (GTA) under GST, which lets freight recovered from customers carry 5% GST rather than 18%. On 22-Jul-2026 the proxy adviser InGovern wrote to SEBI asking whether the risk and any contingent liability were properly disclosed. Meesho says it took legal and accounting opinions, that other horizontal platforms use the same model, and that no tax authority or SEBI has raised it. No amount was quantified; we flag it as a risk, not a cost.

**Advertising** is the profit engine still to come. About two-thirds of sellers by GMV already advertise (Q1FY27 call). Ads lift contribution margin almost one for one because they cost little to serve, and more sellers (+81% in a year) means more bidders. Meesho Mall (~1,200 brands, NMV +93%) brings brands with bigger ad budgets, though Mall orders carry a lower contribution margin for now.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** Valmo is what makes zero commission possible: Meesho delivers cheaper than anyone, so sellers can price lower. But management passes logistics savings to buyers, so Valmo is a growth tool, not a margin tool. The margin case rests on ads. Track contribution margin each quarter: a move back below 4% would mean either logistics trouble or ads not scaling.

sections.title: New initiatives: small bets with a hard ₹200 cr annual loss cap

blocks.p: Meesho reports a second segment, **new initiatives** (its "Horizon 2" bets): a low-cost local logistics network for daily essentials, digital financial services (partner NBFCs lend to sellers and buyers; Meesho gives them a first-loss default guarantee) and AI services. Revenue was only ₹12.2 cr in FY26 against a loss of ₹70 cr; the Q1FY27 loss was ₹39 cr. In Jun-2026 the board approved buying **Kirana Club**, an app that connects FMCG brands and distributors with small retailers in Tier 2+ towns ("Meesho for retailers"), for ~₹202 cr in cash. Management caps total new-initiative losses at ~₹200 cr a year and says the local-logistics bet is still "pre product-market fit".

blocks.callout: **Our view:** we value the new initiatives at the present value of the losses still to come (about four more years at the ₹200 cr cap), not at an option value. Valmo and content commerce both began as Horizon 2 bets and became core, so success would be upside; but the first-loss guarantees in financial services add credit risk that the segment numbers do not yet show.

blocks.callout: **Verdict: a narrow moat built on cost, not on customer captivity.** Meesho is the low-cost operator in Indian e-commerce, with the largest buyer base and the longest tail of unbranded sellers. Neither buyers nor sellers are locked in, and Flipkart and Amazon have copied the zero-commission, low-price format. The moat is real as long as Meesho stays the cheapest, which is why it keeps passing savings on rather than banking them. That limits how high margins can go.

sections.title: Revenue up 16x in five years; losses shrinking but not gone

blocks.p: Meesho's revenue rose from ₹793 cr in FY21 to ₹12,626 cr in FY26 (+34% in FY26). Revenue is mostly what sellers pay for delivery through Meesho's logistics network, plus advertising; Meesho charges sellers no commission, so revenue is ~30% of the value of goods delivered (NMV). Losses peaked at ₹3,248 cr in FY22, fell to ₹328 cr in FY24, and jumped again in FY25 (₹3,942 cr) only because of ~₹3,800 cr of one-off costs from moving the parent company from the US to India. FY26 lost ₹1,358 cr as Meesho spent more to win users and absorbed a costly logistics scale-up. Q1FY27 lost ₹133 cr, the smallest quarterly loss since listing.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** reported EBITDA margins (−12% of revenue in FY26) look worse than the business because revenue is only ~30% of order value. The better yardstick is profit as a share of NMV: marketplace adjusted EBITDA was −2.8% of NMV in FY26 and −1.2% in Q1FY27. Other income (₹416 cr in FY26, interest on ₹6,750 cr of cash) still covers a third of the operating loss. Break-even at the operating level is the next milestone; we expect it in FY28E.

sections.title: Reported vs adjusted: ESOPs, one-offs and treasury income

blocks.p: Meesho's headline profit measure, **adjusted EBITDA**, is the segment result: it leaves out share-based pay (ESOP), exceptional items and other income. In FY26 adjusted EBITDA was −₹1,246 cr; ESOP (₹182 cr), exceptional costs (₹141 cr: costs of the US-to-India merger and a cloud-vendor settlement), depreciation and interest took it to an operating loss of ~₹1,625 cr, and interest on the cash pile (₹416 cr) brought the pre-tax loss to ₹-1,209 cr. Tax of ₹148 cr was paid by profitable subsidiaries even though the group made a loss.

pair.source: Q1FY27 letter (non-GAAP reconciliation)

pair.title: ESOP cost has come down since the FY25 founder grants vested
pair.source: Meesho shareholders' letters and FY26 annual report, GAM Research

bullets: **One-offs were very large in FY25.** Moving the parent from the US to India cost ₹1,346 cr of exceptional items (₹482 cr ESOP-modification charge, ₹62 cr accelerated vesting, ₹734 cr of perquisite tax paid on behalf of the founders, ₹68 cr deal costs) and ₹2,487 cr of tax. Before them FY25 lost only ~₹108 cr before tax. Investors should compare FY24 → FY26 on adjusted EBITDA, not on reported profit.

**ESOP is a real cost.** 17.9 cr option shares (~3.9% of the company) were outstanding at Mar-26 at a ₹1 exercise price. We count them in the share count (474.3 cr) and charge ₹170-210 cr a year of ESOP cost in our forecasts.
**Other income props up the bottom line.** Treasury income (₹416 cr in FY26) covered a third of the operating loss. It falls if cash is spent; it is not a business profit.

**Revenue presentation changed in FY26.** From 15-Mar-2025 Meesho piloted a model in which some last-mile partners billed sellers directly (Meesho booked only a facilitation fee), then reverted to the old model during FY26. Revenue as a % of NMV moved with it; compare growth on NMV.
**Contingent liabilities are large.** Income-tax demands of ₹2,072 cr (AY2022-23 and AY2023-24) are under appeal and not provided for; a ₹14 cr GST demand was upheld on first appeal (Apr-2026).

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** The company reconciles every adjusted figure and reports free cash flow, which is good practice. But large one-offs, ESOPs paid in shares, unprovided tax demands of ~30% of cash and the GST question over Valmo's freight make reported numbers harder to rely on than the NMV story suggests.

sections.title: Cash: ₹6,521 cr, no debt, and sellers fund the working capital

blocks.p: Meesho held ₹6,521 cr of cash, bank deposits and treasury investments at Jun-2026 (company figure) and has no borrowings beyond ₹63 cr of leases. The IPO (Dec-2025) brought in ₹4,125 cr net of costs, but ₹3,344 cr went on one-time costs of the re-domicile (mainly ₹2,780 cr of income tax paid in FY26), so cash rose only from ₹6,593 cr to ₹6,750 cr over FY26. Working capital is negative: Meesho collects from buyers before it pays sellers and logistics partners, so growth releases cash. Screener's "cash + investments" (₹3,103 cr at Mar-26) is lower than the company figure because ~₹3,647 cr of bank deposits sit inside other assets.

sections.title: Ownership: venture investors selling, Indian funds buying

blocks.p: Meesho has founder-promoters with a small stake (16.4% at Jun-2026: Vidit Aatrey and Sanjeev Kumar) and a register still dominated by its venture backers, who sit in the 'public' bucket because they are not promoters. The six-month lock-in on pre-IPO holders ended on 9-Jun-2026; since then Indian mutual funds have been the main buyers.

blocks.callout: **What this means:** the free float is growing fast as venture investors sell after the lock-in (Fidelity sold 5.98 cr shares on 10-Jun-2026; Y Combinator sold ~1% in Aug-2026), and domestic funds are absorbing it (domestic institutions 5.6% → 9.1% in one quarter). Venture investors still own close to 40%: further block sales are an overhang on the price until the next lock-in milestone (Jun-2027). Promoters own only ~16%, so their economic interest is modest, although their ESOPs add to it.

blocks.p: Our NMV growth sits in the middle of the street (23-30%). Our margins are at the low end: we have the marketplace at 1.3% of NMV in FY29E, below Citi (2.1%) and below the 3-4% that most brokers expect by FY30-31. The difference is our view that Meesho will keep reinvesting logistics savings in lower prices. A consensus EPS series is not meaningful while the company is loss-making; brokers value Meesho on NMV, out-year EBITDA or a DCF.

blocks.p: The street is split. 9 of 16 brokers rate Meesho a Buy, on the case that it is the only scaled value platform, that ads are under-monetised (J.P. Morgan: 1.8% of NMV vs 3.7% globally) and that operating leverage will follow. The sceptics (JM Financial, Nomura, CLSA, Macquarie) argue that falling order values cap unit economics, that the price already discounts years of fast growth and margin gains, and that Flipkart, Amazon and quick commerce are closing in. The LSEG median target was ₹215 (16 analysts) on 25-Sep-2026; our own table gives ₹213. The disclosed methods are EV/NMV (Jefferies), EV/EBITDA on FY29-31E discounted back (MOFSL, J.P. Morgan, Citi, BofA), EV/sales (Choice) and DCF (Ventura, JM Financial).

blocks.p: Meesho makes losses, so P/E cannot be used. Brokers value it on order value (EV/NMV), on EBITDA two to five years out discounted back, on EV/sales, or with a DCF. blocks.h: Our marketplace multiple: 1.2x NMV, and why

blocks.p: Meesho listed on 10-Dec-2025, so its own history is short. Following our rule for recent listings (HYUNDAI, HDBFS, TENNIND), we skip the listing month, when the stock traded at an IPO premium (median 1.52x, peak 1.94x forward NMV), and use every daily close from 1-Jan-2026 to 30-Sep-2026: 185 closes, nine months rather than the usual twelve. We pair it with the sector's move over the same window.

**New initiatives:** Start-up losses valued as the present value of losses still to come: ~₹200 cr a year (the budget cap) for four more years at 13.1% (annuity factor 3.0); bull two years (1.7), bear six years (4.0). Any value of a business that does succeed is upside.

**Kirana Club purchase price:** Board approved on 12-Jun-2026: ~₹202 cr in cash for 100% of Kirana Club (B2B marketplace for small retailers), paid in three tranches to complete by 31-Mar-2027. Not yet in the model's Mar-27 cash; its losses sit inside new initiatives.

**Contested income-tax demands:** Income-tax demands of ₹1,500 cr (AY2023-24) and ₹572 cr (AY2022-23, stayed by the Karnataka High Court) are contested and not provided for (AR FY26 note 29). Base and bull: nil (company has appealed); bear: paid in full.
**Net cash at end-FY27E:** Model forecast: cash, bank deposits and treasury investments less lease liabilities at Mar-27.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a strong franchise at a full price

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's largest e-commerce platform by buyers and orders, growing NMV ~30%, with a real cost advantage (zero commission, Valmo), ₹6,521 cr of cash and a business that funds its own growth. Our sum of the parts gives {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).

**What you are paying for:** ~₹1,08,024 cr of market value for a marketplace that still loses 1.2% of NMV. The price implies ~1.35x our Sep-28E NMV, above the stock's own median (1.23x) since January and our 1.2x. To justify it, ads must lift margins to the street's 3-4% of NMV by FY30-31 while growth stays above 25%. We think margins rise more slowly because Meesho reinvests its savings in lower prices.
